articles.title: Better Go Mad in the Wild review – boozing, bantering hermits impart their spiritual wisdom
articles.summary: Director Miro Remo journeys deep into the Czech countryside to find two brothers living an isolated life filled with quixotic wisdom in this surreal documentary. Narrated by a slaughtered bull, this extraordinary film takes the less-travelled path in charting the daily life of a pair of Czech twins…
body: Closing on 60, “Franta” and “Ondra” still farm their smallholding with the help of Nandy, a mutinous bull ill-chosen as a draught animal. In their downtime, they booze, banter and bicker, lament their lack of prospects with the fairer sex, and blow off steam in epic arm-wrestling bouts. Despite an arm lost to a sawmill accident, it’s Franta who’s usually the victor; he is also possessed by a quixotic streak absent in his bluff sibling. Letting loose streams of poetry into the air like bunting, wishing “joy to all conscious beings”, he is also constructing his own Da Vinci-style perpetual flying machine. “Your aversion to my perpetuum is a little annoying,” he informs the exasperated Ondra.

articles.title: ‘It’s not good to walk through the world feeling like prey’: Thelma & Louise’s writer on turning a movie classic into a musical
articles.summary: It was her very first film and it won her an Oscar. But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs? She talks about what made her write it – and how little has changed since.
body: ‘I have a world-class case of beginner’s luck,” says Callie Khouri, who won an Oscar for her very first screenplay, Thelma & Louise. She also scored a hit with her first TV series, Nashville, which lasted six seasons. And at 68, she is taking on another first by penning a musical theatre version of Thelma & Louise, hoping her luck hasn’t run out. “I hope that this is not the end of that streak,” she laughs. “That I don’t hit a wall here and slide down it like Wile E Coyote.”

I meet Khouri at a south London studio during one of the summer’s heatwaves. She is dressed in airy, white cotton, looking like an elegant lady who might be tending her garden in the American south – which is what she spends a lot of her time doing these days at home in Nashville, Tennessee, with husband T-Bone Burnett. When Khouri floated the idea for the musical at home, it was record producer Burnett who immediately suggested a composer, the American singer-songwriter Neko Case.

But can Callie Khouri now make it work on stage with songs?

articles.title: Balanga Secures First International Sales for History Doc ‘Beasts of the Colosseum,’ Ahead of Unifrance Rendez-Vous (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: International distributor Balanga has announced its first major international sales of its documentary “Beasts of the Colosseum,” produced by Antoine Henriquet’s AH! Production and Jean-Luc Berlot’s Adline for Novo 19 in France, in association with Mediaset in Italy.
body: “The film explores the moment when nature stopped being simply observed or studied, and began to be staged, dramatized and consumed as entertainment,” Bochnacki added.
The doc world premiered out of competition at the Cannes AI Film Festival, and will have its first screening for international buyers at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre on September 8.
Variety had a chance to interview the doc’s producer, Enora Contant, ahead of its screening at Unifrance Rendez-Vous.

Enora Contant: Like many viewers, I was deeply struck by the tiger scene in Ridley Scott’s “Gladiator.” It brought back those stories we first encounter at school – of men being thrown to wild beasts in Roman arenas – which fascinate us as much as they terrify us. And yet, one question is rarely asked: Where did all these animals come from? We know a great deal about the fate of the men who took part in the Roman games, but far less about the animals themselves.

articles.title: Venice Horizons Winner Anuparna Roy Returns to Lido With Mumbai Story of Migrants, Desire and Belonging ‘Lovers in the Blue Night’
articles.summary: Indian filmmaker Anuparna Roy has been carrying Ameena’s story since childhood. Ameena was a bonded laborer in Roy’s hometown, and something she once said about her marriage stayed with the director long after she grew up and moved away.
body: Roy says “Songs of Forgotten Trees” was a personal story made under difficult funding conditions, built around two women who barely leave a single house. “Lovers in the Blue Night” widens that frame to four migrants moving through Mumbai; she also describes the production itself as far more professional this time, with deadlines and limitations she is still learning to work inside.

Asked whether she expected the new film to move into Venice’s main competition rather in Horizons, Roy says she dreamed of it rather than expected it, and that landing in the section again is no disappointment. She still considers herself a new director learning her craft alongside filmmakers she admires.

Ameena’s arc did not stay fixed to the facts that Roy remembered. She says her early instinct was rebellious, imagining the character finding real love and leaving her marriage behind. But that path stopped looking like simple freedom as the script developed. “That is also another loop — another loop of patriarchy,” Roy says, describing what looks from the outside like an escape into a happy ending.

articles.title: Amazon’s Newest Fire Tablet Is Only $150, With 10,000 Units Sold In the Last Month Alone
articles.summary: Amazon has made a name for itself with its slate of Alexa-enabled devices, but the retail giant is also a leader when it comes to its lineup of tablets. Whether for work or streaming, Amazon’s Fire Tablets offer up huge value, especially when compared to Apple’s iPad or the Samsung Galaxy Tab.
body: The Fire Tablet features a 10.1-inch full HD display with millions of dazzling pixels that bring your content to life in full, vivid color. Amazon says the Fire HD 10 is almost 20% brighter than the Samsung Galaxy Tab A8 when comparing the two side by side.
With up to 13 hours of battery life, meantime, the Amazon Fire Tablet beats the iPad by three extra hours, letting you spend more time connected to your device and less time waiting for it to charge.

Features-wise, the HD 10 Tablet comes with 32GB of storage, a super fast octa-core processor (that offers “25% faster performance than the previous generation,” per Amazon) and 4GB of RAM for instant responsiveness and smooth loading of all your apps and content.

The 5MP front-facing camera is great for taking calls, while the 5MP rear-facing cameras can be used for snapping photos or shooting video in stunning 1080p HD quality. The tablet is great for streaming too, with Dolby Atmos sound and a large, crisp display.

articles.title: Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller on Making ICE Doc ‘They’re Here’ Like a “Horror Movie”
articles.summary: The Oscar-winning filmmaker and Minneapolis-based journalist chronicle the Minneapolis resistance movement to ICE’s paramilitary occupation, which resulted in the fatal shootings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti.
body: That’s the message of Oscar-winning documentarian Laura Poitras, whose new short documentary They’re Here chronicles how Immigration Customs Enforcement troops invaded and occupied Minneapolis last year, and the anonymous residents who resisted.

Stylistically, the film draws from horror and sci-fi cinema to depict how a picturesque American Midwestern city is turned into a dystopian nightmare. Men in balaclavas in unmarked cars drive down quiet snowy streets. At the Minneapolis airport, American vacationers gaze out the windows at shackled prisoners being dragged onboard planes nearby. A husband and wife hide in the trunk of a car as their son tries to sneak them past ICE officers.

They’re Here is Poitras’s first project since her Nan Goldin documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed, which won the festival’s Golden Lion in 2022 and later earned an Oscar nomination. Poitras previously won the best documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, her landmark account of Edward Snowden and his NSA surveillance disclosures.

articles.title: The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias review – Slavoj Žižek goes in search of paradise
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Inserting himself into settings from Apocalypse Now to The Handmaid’s Tale, the pop-cultural critic finds it hard to locate the perfect ending – even with spoilers.
body: The great pop-cultural critic and postmodern Marxist is back, with more entertaining and semi-serious provocations and deconstructive insights, notionally into the idea of “utopias”, as they appear in the movies and TV, having already done “cinema” and “ideology”.

I was incidentally hoping for a Slavoj Žižek aria about how unexpectedly great and profoundly important threequels are. This is of course delivered emphatically in that amazing voice, now as universally recognised as Werner Herzog’s. Is it too late for a cameo on The Simpsons?

Žižek’s trademarked and now slightly overworked way with a paradox is again in evidence. (He says that “A communist should be a convinced pessimist …” and actually describes himself as a communist though lays off the bet in his tongue-in-cheek way by saying that this he knows “this sounds crazy”.

He isn’t above being a bit paradoxical himself – at one point praising The Rapture (1991) as showing the apocalypse as the literal real thing and not some lame metaphor, and then praising Last Year At Marienbad (1961) for disclosing the truth of a post-apocalyptic state of endless return.

articles.title: How colourful stripes (and rubber chickens) helped Paul Smith conquer the fashion world
articles.summary: As he publishes his autobiography, Sir Paul Smith takes BBC News on a tour of his London headquarters.
body: Sir Paul Smith, the doyen of British fashion, is flailing around in his office with two large rubber chickens and making them squeak them with gusto.
"The chickens are the reason I was successful in Japan," he explains.

articles.title: Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin and Charli XCX says bye to Brat - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist
articles.summary: Nominees for the Abbey Road awards captured some of the past year's best moments in music.
body: Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Photography Awards.
The awards, which this year considered works by more than 24,500 submissions from 42 different countries, released a shortlist of 40 finalists across eight categories on Tuesday.

The likes of Kendrick Lamar, Fontaines DC, Tame Impala and Sombr also feature in the shots, while other images of stars including FKA Twigs have been selected - out of competition - for judges' awards.
All of the finalist photographs will go on display in the LED tunnel at entertainment complex Outernet London from 8 to 14 September.
